Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity
Stack-Based O(N) O(N)
  • Why O(N)?
    • Step 2: Finding the potential celebrity takes O(N).
    • Step 3: Verifying the celebrity takes O(N).
  • Why O(N) Space?
    • We use a stack of size O(N).

Notes:

  • The stack-based approach reduces comparisons from O(N²) to O(N).
  • The matrix is guaranteed to have 0s on diagonal (no self-knowledge).
  • Efficient for party sizes up to 100 as per constraints.

Problem Statement: 158¶

Restrictive Candy Crush Given a string s and an integer k, the task is to reduce the string by applying the following operation:

  • Choose a group of k consecutive identical characters and remove them.

The operation can be performed any number of times until it is no longer possible.

Explanation

  • "aa" is removed → "bbcc"
  • "bb" is removed → "cc"
  • "cc" is removed → ""
  • Final result: "" (empty string)

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ |s| ≤ 10^5
  • 1 ≤ k ≤ |s|
  • s consists of lowercase English letters only.

Example
Input: s = "deeedbbcccbdaa", k = 3
Output: "aa"
Explanation:

  • Remove "eee" → "ddbbcccbdaa"
  • Remove "bbb" → "ddccdaa"
  • Remove "ccc" → "dddaa"
  • Remove "ddd" → "aa"

Input:

  • Integer k
  • String s

Output:

  • Reduced string after all possible removals

Goal:
To reduce the string by removing consecutive groups of k identical characters using an efficient algorithm.

Approach:
Use a stack to store pairs of (character, frequency). Iterate through the string, updating frequencies, and remove groups when frequency reaches k.

Optimal Approach: Using a Stack Key Observations

  1. Use a stack to track consecutive characters and their frequency.
  2. If a character reaches k occurrences, remove them from the stack.
  3. Build the final string from the stack.

Algorithm

  1. Use a stack to store pairs of (character, frequency).
  2. Iterate through s:
    • If the stack is empty or the top character is different, push (char, 1).
    • If the top character matches the current character:
      • Increase the frequency.
      • If frequency reaches k, remove the group.
  3. Build the final string from the stack.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Initialize empty stack
  • For each character in string:
    • If stack is empty or top char != current char, push (char,1)
    • Else increment frequency of top pair
    • If frequency == k, pop the pair
  • Construct result from stack
  • End

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

initialize empty stack S
for char in s:
if S is empty or S.top.char != char:
push (char, 1)
else:
increment S.top.frequency
if S.top.frequency == k:
pop S.top
build result string by repeating chars in stack pairs
return result

Code Implementation (Java)

class Solution
{
    public static String reduced_String(int k, String s)
    {
        // Your code goes here
        Stack<Character> st=new Stack<>();
        int i=0;
        while(i < s.length()){
            char ch=s.charAt(i++);
            st.push(ch);
            int count=0;
            while(st.size() >0 && st.peek()==ch){
                count++;
                st.pop();
            }
            
            if(count==k){
                continue;
            }
            else{
                while(count>0){
                st.push(ch);
                count--;
                }
            }
        }
        
        StringBuilder ans=new StringBuilder();
        for(char c: st){
             ans.append(c);
        }
        
        return ans.toString();
    }
}

Approach:2(Using a Stack of Pairs)

import java.util.*;

public class GfG {
    static String removeKChar(int k, String str) {
        if (k == 1) return "";

        StringBuilder ans = new StringBuilder();
        Stack<Pair<Character, Integer>> stk = new Stack<>();

        for (char c : str.toCharArray()) {
            if (stk.isEmpty()) {
                stk.push(new Pair<>(c, 1));
            } else {
                if (c == stk.peek().getKey()) {
                    Pair<Character, Integer> p = stk.pop();
                    if (p.getValue() + 1 < k) stk.push(new Pair<>(p.getKey(), p.getValue() + 1));
                } else {
                    stk.push(new Pair<>(c, 1));
                }
            }
        }

        while (!stk.isEmpty()) {
            Pair<Character, Integer> top = stk.pop();
            for (int i = 0; i < top.getValue(); i++) {
                ans.append(top.getKey());
            }
        }

        return ans.reverse().toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s = "geeksforgeeks";
        int k = 2;
        System.out.println(removeKChar(k, s));
    }
}

class Pair<K, V> {
    private K key;
    private V value;

    public Pair(K key, V value) {
        this.key = key;
        this.value = value;
    }

    public K getKey() { return key; }
    public V getValue() { return value; }
}

Time and Space Complexity

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity
Stack-Based O(N) O(N)
  • Why O(N)?
    • We iterate through s once.
    • Stack operations (push/pop) are O(1) each.
  • Why O(N) Space?
    • The stack stores at most N elements in the worst case.

Notes:

  • If k=1, entire string reduces to empty string.
  • String reconstruction is done from the stack in reverse order.
  • Two main approaches: character stack with manual counting, or stack of (char, count) pairs.

Problem Statement: 157¶

Count the Reversals You are given a string S consisting of only opening { and closing } curly brackets.
Your task is to find the minimum number of reversals required to convert S into a balanced expression.

Reversal Definition A reversal means changing { to } or vice-versa.

Explanation

  • The given string cannot be balanced by any number of reversals.

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ |S| ≤ 10^5
  • The input string consists of only { and }.

Example
Input: "}{{}}{{{"
Output: 3
Explanation: After 3 reversals, the expression becomes balanced.

Input:

  • A string S of { and } characters

Output:

  • Minimum number of reversals required or -1 if impossible

Goal:
Determine the minimum reversals to balance the bracket expression.

Approach: Using a Stack Algorithm

  1. Check for odd length

    • If |S| is odd, return -1 (impossible to balance).

  2. Use a Stack to track unbalanced brackets

    • Traverse the string:
      • If opening {, push it to the stack.
      • If closing }:
        • If the stack is not empty, pop an opening {} (pair matched).
        • Else, push a { (treat this as an unbalanced bracket).

  3. Calculate the required reversals

    • Let stackSize = count of unbalanced brackets left in stack
    • If stackSize is odd, return -1 (cannot balance).
    • Otherwise:
      • ans = (unbalanced opening {) / 2 + (unbalanced closing }) / 2

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Check length parity (odd → return -1)
  • Traverse string pushing { and popping on } if possible
  • Count unmatched brackets in stack
  • Calculate reversals based on counts

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

if length of S is odd:
return -1
initialize stack
for char in S:
if char == '{':
push onto stack
else: # char == '}'
if stack not empty:
pop stack
else:
push '{' onto stack
increment reversal count by 1
if stack size is odd:
return -1
return reversal count + stack.size() / 2

Code Implementation (Java)

import java.util.*;

class Sol {
    int countRev(String s) {
        // Step 1: If the length is odd, it is impossible to balance
        if (s.length() % 2 != 0) return -1;

        Stack<Character> st = new Stack<>();
        int ans = 0;

        // Step 2: Traverse the string
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char ch = s.charAt(i);

            if (ch == '{') {
                st.push(ch);
            } else {
                // If stack is not empty, pop an opening `{`
                if (!st.isEmpty()) {
                    st.pop();
                } else {
                    // If stack is empty, treat `}` as an unbalanced `{`
                    st.push('{');
                    ans++;
                }
            }
        }

        // Step 3: If the stack size is odd, return -1
        if (st.size() % 2 != 0) return -1;

        // Step 4: Add half of remaining unbalanced brackets
        ans += st.size() / 2;
        return ans;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity
Stack-Based O(N) O(N)
  • Why O(N)?
    • We traverse the string once O(N).
    • Stack operations (push/pop) are O(1) each.
  • Why O(N) Space?
    • In the worst case, the stack stores all brackets.

Notes:

  • Odd length strings cannot be balanced, return -1 immediately.
  • Counting and treating unmatched } as { during traversal simplifies logic.
  • Final answer includes reversals counted during traversal plus half the remaining unmatched brackets.

Problem Statement: 159¶

Queue Using Array Implement a Queue using an Array. The queue should support the following operations:

  1. Push (1 x) → Insert element x into the queue.
  2. Pop (2) → Remove and return the front element of the queue.
    • If the queue is empty, return -1.

Note:

  • Implement only the push() and pop() functions.
  • The driver code will handle input and output.

Explanation

  • 1 2 → Push 2
  • 1 3 → Push 3
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 2
  • 1 4 → Push 4
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 3

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ Q ≤ 100000
  • 1 ≤ x ≤ 100000

Example
Input sequence:


1 2  (push 2)
1 3  (push 3)
2    (pop) → returns 2
1 4  (push 4)
2    (pop) → returns 3

Input:

  • A series of commands either 1 x to push or 2 to pop.

Output:

  • Return popped elements or -1 if queue is empty.

Goal:
Efficiently implement queue operations using an array.

Approach: Implementing Queue Using an Array Key Observations

  1. We use an array arr[] to store queue elements.
  2. Maintain front and rear pointers:
    • front → Points to the first element.
    • rear → Points to the next insertion position.
  3. Push (1 x)
    • Insert x at arr[rear].
    • Increment rear.
  4. Pop (2)
    • Return arr[front] and increment front.
    • If queue is empty, return -1.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start → On push: arr[rear] = x, rear++ → On pop: if front == rear return -1 else return arr[front], front++

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

Initialize front = 0, rear = 0
push(x):
if rear == array length: // overflow check
return
arr\[rear] = x
rear++

pop():
if front == rear:
return -1
val = arr\[front]
front++
return val

Code Implementation (Java)

class MyQueue {
    int front, rear;
    int arr[] = new int[100005]; // Fixed-size array

    MyQueue() {
        front = 0;
        rear = 0;
    }
    
    // Function to push an element x into the queue.
    void push(int x) {
        if (rear == arr.length) return; // Prevent overflow
        arr[rear] = x;
        rear++;
    } 

    // Function to pop an element from queue and return that element.
    int pop() {
        if (front == rear) return -1; // Queue empty
        int result = arr[front];
        front++;
        return result;
    } 
}

Time and Space Complexity

Operation Time Complexity Space Complexity
Push (1 x) O(1) O(N)
Pop (2) O(1) O(N)
  • Why O(1)?
    • Insertion (push) and deletion (pop) take constant time.
  • Why O(N) Space?
    • We use an array of size N.

Notes:

  • No dynamic resizing; fixed array size assumed.
  • Overflow handled by ignoring push if array is full.
  • Front and rear pointers move forward, no wrap-around or circular queue logic used.

Problem Statement: Array Implementation of Queue - Simple¶

Implement a queue using Java's built-in data structures and provide basic queue operations like enqueue, dequeue, checking if empty, getting the front element, and displaying the queue.

Example:

Operations:
enqueue(1)
enqueue(2)
enqueue(3)
getFront() -> 1
dequeue()
enqueue(4)
display() -> 2 3 4

Input:
Sequence of queue operations: enqueue, dequeue, getFront, display.

Output:

  • For getFront(), return the front element or -1 if queue is empty.
  • For display(), print all queue elements in order.

Constraints:

  • Queue size can be dynamic (using LinkedList).
  • Operations should be efficient.

Goal:
Implement a queue supporting the above operations simply and efficiently.

Approach:
Use Java's LinkedList class which implements the Queue interface to manage the queue elements. The linked list handles dynamic size and provides O(1) time for enqueue and dequeue operations.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

Initialize queue q as LinkedList

function isEmpty():
return q.isEmpty()

function enqueue(x):
q.add(x)

function dequeue():
if not isEmpty():
q.poll()

function getFront():
if isEmpty():
return -1
else:
return q.peek()

function display():
for element in q:
print element

Code

import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.Queue;

class MyQueue {
    private Queue<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>();

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return q.isEmpty();
    }

    public void enqueue(int x) {
        q.add(x);
    }

    public void dequeue() {
        if (!isEmpty()) q.poll();
    }

    public int getFront() {
        return isEmpty() ? -1 : q.peek();
    }

    public void display() {
        for (int x : q) System.out.print(x + " ");
        System.out.println();
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyQueue q = new MyQueue();
        q.enqueue(1);
        q.enqueue(2);
        q.enqueue(3);
        System.out.println(q.getFront());  // Output: 1
        q.dequeue();
        q.enqueue(4);
        q.display();  // Output: 2 3 4
    }
}

Time Complexity:

  • enqueue and dequeue: O(1)
  • getFront: O(1)
  • display: O(n) where n is number of elements in queue

Space Complexity:

  • O(n), where n is the number of elements in the queue

Notes:

  • Using Java's LinkedList simplifies queue implementation and handles dynamic resizing internally.
  • This implementation is straightforward for educational and practical use.

Problem Statement: 160¶

Implement a Queue using a Linked List. The queue should support the following operations:

  1. Push (1 x) → Insert element x into the queue.
  2. Pop (2) → Remove and return the front element of the queue.
    • If the queue is empty, return -1.

Note:

  • Implement only the push() and pop() functions.
  • The driver code will handle input and output.

Explanation

  • 1 10 → Push 10
  • 1 20 → Push 20
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 10
  • 1 30 → Push 30
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 20

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ Q ≤ 100000
  • 1 ≤ x ≤ 100000

Example
Input sequence:


1 10  (push 10)
1 20  (push 20)
2     (pop) → returns 10
1 30  (push 30)
2     (pop) → returns 20

Input:

  • A series of commands either 1 x to push or 2 to pop.

Output:

  • Return popped elements or -1 if queue is empty.

Goal:
Efficiently implement queue operations using a linked list.

Approach: Implementing Queue Using Linked List Key Observations

  1. Unlike an array-based queue, a linked list queue does not have a fixed size.
  2. Maintain front and rear pointers:
    • front → Points to the first element.
    • rear → Points to the last element.
  3. Push (1 x)
    • Create a new node and add it at the rear.
    • Update the rear pointer.
  4. Pop (2)
    • Remove and return the front element.
    • Update the front pointer.
    • If the queue becomes empty, set rear = null.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start → On push: create node, link rear.next → rear = new node
  • On pop: if front null return -1 else return front.data, front = front.next; if front null rear = null

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

push(a):
newNode = new Node(a)
if rear == null:
front = rear = newNode
return
rear.next = newNode
rear = newNode

pop():
if front == null:
return -1
val = front.data
front = front.next
if front == null:
rear = null
return val

Code Implementation (Java)

class QueueNode {
    int data;
    QueueNode next;
    QueueNode(int a) {
        data = a;
        next = null;
    }
}

class MyQueue {
    QueueNode front, rear;
    
    // Function to push an element into the queue.
    void push(int a) {
        QueueNode newNode = new QueueNode(a);
        
        if (rear == null) {
            front = rear = newNode;
            return;
        }
        
        rear.next = newNode;
        rear = newNode;
    }
    
    // Function to pop front element from the queue.
    int pop() {
        if (front == null) {
            return -1; // Queue is empty
        }
        
        int result = front.data;
        front = front.next;
        
        if (front == null) {
            rear = null; // Queue is now empty
        }
        
        return result;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity

Operation Time Complexity Space Complexity
Push (1 x) O(1) O(N)
Pop (2) O(1) O(N)
  • Why O(1)?
    • Insertion (push) and deletion (pop) take constant time.
  • Why O(N) Space?
    • Each element requires a node (extra memory for pointers).

Notes:

  • No fixed size limit unlike array implementation.
  • Both operations run in constant time.
  • Properly update rear to null when queue becomes empty.

Problem Statement : 161¶

Queue Using Two Stacks Implement a Queue using two stacks (s1 & s2). The queue should support the following operations:

  1. Push (1 x) → Insert element x into the queue.
  2. Pop (2) → Remove and return the front element of the queue.
    • If the queue is empty, return -1.

Note:

  • Implement only the Push() and Pop() functions.
  • The driver code will handle input and output.

Explanation

  • 1 10 → Push 10
  • 1 20 → Push 20
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 10
  • 1 30 → Push 30
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 20

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ Q ≤ 100000
  • 1 ≤ x ≤ 100000

Example
Input sequence:


1 10  (push 10)
1 20  (push 20)
2     (pop) → returns 10
1 30  (push 30)
2     (pop) → returns 20

Input:

  • Commands in the form 1 x for push and 2 for pop.

Output:

  • Return popped element or -1 if queue is empty.

Goal:
Implement efficient queue operations using two stacks.

Approach: Implementing Queue Using Two Stacks

  • Use two stacks, s1 for push and s2 for pop operations.
  • Push directly onto s1.
  • Pop from s2 if not empty; if empty, transfer all elements from s1 to s2 and then pop.

Key Observations

  1. A Queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out).
  2. A Stack follows LIFO (Last In, First Out).
  3. We simulate FIFO behavior using two stacks:
    • s1 → Used for push operations.
    • s2 → Used for pop operations.

Push Operation (1 x)

  1. Simply push x onto s1.

Time Complexity: O(1)

Pop Operation (2)

  1. If s2 is not empty, pop from s2.
  2. Otherwise:
    • Transfer all elements from s1 → s2 (reversing order).
    • Pop from s2.
  3. If both stacks are empty, return -1.

Time Complexity:

  • Worst Case (O(N)) (when transferring s1 → s2).
  • Amortized (O(1)) over multiple operations.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Push: s1.push(x)
  • Pop: if s2 empty, transfer all from s1 to s2, then pop s2; else pop s2
  • If both empty return -1

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

Push(x):
s1.push(x)

Pop():
if s1 empty and s2 empty:
return -1
if s2 empty:
while s1 not empty:
s2.push(s1.pop())
return s2.pop()

Code Implementation (Java)

class StackQueue {
    Stack<Integer> s1 = new Stack<>();
    Stack<Integer> s2 = new Stack<>();

    // Function to push an element into queue
    void Push(int x) {
        s1.push(x);
    }

    // Function to pop front element from queue
    int Pop() {
        if (s1.isEmpty() && s2.isEmpty()) {
            return -1; // Queue is empty
        }

        if (s2.isEmpty()) {
            while (!s1.isEmpty()) {
                s2.push(s1.pop());
            }
        }
        
        return s2.pop();
    }
}

Time Complexity:

  • Push: O(1)
  • Pop: Amortized O(1), Worst case O(N) when transferring stacks

Space Complexity:

  • O(N) for two stacks combined

Notes:

  • Amortized analysis explains why pop operation is efficient overall.
  • Ensures queue behavior using stack operations.

Problem Statement: 162¶

Stack Using Two Queues Implement a Stack using two queues (q1 and q2). The stack should support the following operations:

  1. Push (1 x) → Insert element x into the stack.
  2. Pop (2) → Remove and return the top element of the stack.
    • If the stack is empty, return -1.

Note:

  • Implement only the push() and pop() functions.
  • The driver code will handle input and output.

Explanation

  • 1 10 → Push 10
  • 1 20 → Push 20
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 20 (LIFO)
  • 1 30 → Push 30
  • 2 → Pop → Returns 30

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ Q ≤ 100000
  • 1 ≤ x ≤ 100000

Example
Input sequence:


1 10  (push 10)
1 20  (push 20)
2     (pop) → returns 20
1 30  (push 30)
2     (pop) → returns 30

Input:

  • Commands in the form 1 x for push and 2 for pop.

Output:

  • Return popped element or -1 if stack is empty.

Goal:
Simulate stack operations (LIFO) using two FIFO queues.

Approach: Implementing Stack Using Two Queues

  • Use two queues, q1 for main storage and q2 as temporary helper.
  • Push: enqueue directly into q1.
  • Pop: dequeue all elements except last from q1 into q2, then dequeue last element from q1 (top of stack). Swap q1 and q2.

Key Observations

  1. A Stack follows LIFO (Last In, First Out).
  2. A Queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out).
  3. We simulate LIFO behavior using two queues:
    • q1 → Stores the stack elements.
    • q2 → Used as a temporary queue.

Push Operation (1 x)

  1. Simply enqueue x into q1.

Time Complexity: O(1)

Pop Operation (2)

  1. Move all elements except the last from q1 → q2.
  2. Remove the last element from q1 (stack's top).
  3. Swap q1 and q2.

Time Complexity: O(N)

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

push(x):
q1.enqueue(x)

pop():
if q1.empty():
return -1
while q1.size() > 1:
q2.enqueue(q1.dequeue())
top = q1.dequeue()
swap(q1, q2)
return top

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Push: enqueue into q1
  • Pop: move all but last from q1 to q2; dequeue last from q1; swap q1 and q2

Code Implementation (Java)

class Queues {
    Queue<Integer> q1 = new LinkedList<>();
    Queue<Integer> q2 = new LinkedList<>();
    
    // Function to push an element into stack using two queues.
    void push(int a) {
        q1.add(a);
    }
    
    // Function to pop an element from stack using two queues. 
    int pop() {
        if (q1.isEmpty()) {
            return -1; // Stack is empty
        }
        
        while (q1.size() > 1) {
            q2.add(q1.poll());
        }
        
        int topElement = q1.poll();
        Queue<Integer> temp = q1;
        q1 = q2;
        q2 = temp;
        
        return topElement;
    }
}

Time Complexity:

  • Push: O(1)
  • Pop: O(N) due to moving elements between queues

Space Complexity:

  • O(N) for storing elements in queues

Notes:

  • This approach emphasizes simulating stack's LIFO using FIFO queues by rearranging elements during pop.

Problem Statement:163¶

Queue Reversal Given a queue q containing integer elements, your task is to reverse the queue.

Explanation

  • The original queue is: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
  • After reversal: 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5 (Number of elements in the queue)
  • 0 ≤ Elements in queue ≤ 10^6

Example
Input:
Queue: 1 2 3 4 5
Output:
Queue: 5 4 3 2 1

Input:

  • A queue q of N integers.

Output:

  • A queue with elements in reverse order.

Goal:
Transform the queue so that the front becomes the rear and vice versa.

Approach We can reverse the queue using two main approaches:

1. Using a Stack (O(N) Time, O(N) Space)

  1. Push all elements of the queue into a stack (LIFO property).
  2. Pop elements from the stack and enqueue them back into the queue.
  3. The queue will now be reversed.

🔹 Time Complexity: O(N) (Each element is pushed and popped once)
🔹 Space Complexity: O(N) (For the stack)

2. Using Recursion (O(N) Time, O(N) Space)

  1. Recursively remove the front element until the queue is empty.
  2. On returning, insert each element at the back.

🔹 Time Complexity: O(N) (Each element is enqueued and dequeued once)
🔹 Space Complexity: O(N) (Recursive call stack)

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Step 1: Enqueue → Stack (LIFO)
  • Step 2: Stack pop → Queue enqueue (Reversed)

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function reverseQueue(q):
create an empty stack
while q is not empty:
stack.push(q.dequeue())
while stack is not empty:
q.enqueue(stack.pop())
return q

Code Implementation (Java) Using a Stack

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    // Function to reverse the queue.
    public Queue<Integer> reverseQueue(Queue<Integer> queue) {
        Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();
        
        // Push all elements to stack
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            stack.push(queue.poll());
        }
        
        // Pop from stack and enqueue back to queue
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            queue.add(stack.pop());
        }
        
        return queue;
    }
}

Notes:

  • Can be done iteratively with a stack or recursively using the call stack.
  • Use recursion only if input size is guaranteed to be small (to avoid stack overflow).

Problem Statement: 164¶

Gas Station Problem There are some gas stations along a circular route. You are given two integer arrays:

  • gas[]: Represents the amount of gas at each station.
  • cost[]: Represents the cost of travelling to the next station.

You have a car with an unlimited gas tank but start the journey with an empty tank.
Your task is to find the starting gas station index from which you can complete the circular journey without running out of gas.

  • If it is not possible, return -1.
  • If a solution exists, it is guaranteed to be unique.

Explanation

  • If you start at station 3 (0-based index):
    • Gas collected: 4, cost to next: 1 → Remaining 3
    • Gas collected: 5, cost to next: 2 → Remaining 6
    • Gas collected: 1, cost to next: 3 → Remaining 4
    • Gas collected: 2, cost to next: 4 → Remaining 2
    • Gas collected: 3, cost to next: 5 → Remaining 0
  • Successfully returned to station 3.

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
  • 0 ≤ gas[i], cost[i] ≤ 10^4

Example
Input:


gas = \[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
cost = \[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]

Output:


3

Goal:
Find the unique starting index (if any) from which a complete circular trip is possible without running out of fuel.

Approach 1. Greedy Approach (O(N) Time, O(1) Space)

  1. Calculate total gas and total cost:
    • If totalGas < totalCost, return -1 (impossible to complete the circuit).
  2. Iterate through stations:
    • Maintain a tank variable to track available gas.
    • If tank becomes negative, reset the starting station to i+1 and reset tank to 0.
  3. Return the start station if totalGas ≥ totalCost.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:


\[Start] → For each station i:
|
↓
totalGas += gas\[i]
totalCost += cost\[i]
tank += gas\[i] - cost\[i]
|
↓
If tank < 0 → start = i+1, tank = 0
|
↓
\[End]
Return start if totalGas >= totalCost else -1

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function startStation(gas, cost):
totalGas = 0
totalCost = 0
tank = 0
start = 0

for i from 0 to length of gas:
    totalGas += gas[i]
    totalCost += cost[i]
    tank += gas[i] - cost[i]

    if tank < 0:
        start = i + 1
        tank = 0

if totalGas >= totalCost:
    return start
else:
    return -1

Code Implementation (Java)

class Solution {
    public int startStation(int[] gas, int[] cost) {
        int totalGas = 0, totalCost = 0;
        int tank = 0, start = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < gas.length; i++) {
            totalGas += gas[i];
            totalCost += cost[i];
            tank += gas[i] - cost[i];

            // If we can't reach the next station
            if (tank < 0) {
                start = i + 1;  // Reset the start position
                tank = 0;       // Reset the tank
            }
        }
        return (totalGas >= totalCost) ? start : -1;
    }
}

🔹 Time Complexity: O(N) (Single pass)
🔹 Space Complexity: O(1) (Constant space)

Notes:

  • The solution is guaranteed to be unique if it exists.
  • This greedy approach works because any failed segment cannot be part of a successful start.

Problem Statement: 165¶

Stream First Non-Repeating Character Given an input stream s consisting only of lowercase alphabets, you need to determine the first non-repeating character at each position from start till i.

  • If there are multiple non-repeating characters, return the first one.
  • If no such character exists, return #.

Explanation

  • a appears → "a"
  • a appears again → "a#" (no unique character)
  • b appears → "a#b"
  • c appears → "a#bb"

Example
Input:


s = "aabc"

Output:


"a#bb"

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ |s| ≤ 10^5
  • Stream contains only lowercase English letters.

Goal:
For each character in the stream, return the first non-repeating character seen so far. If none exist at that point, return #.

Approach 1. Using Queue and Frequency Count (O(N))

  1. Maintain a queue to keep track of characters in the order they appear.
  2. Use a frequency array (count[26]) to track occurrences of each character.
  3. For each character:
    • Increase its frequency.
    • Add to queue if it's the first occurrence.
    • Remove elements from the queue until the front has frequency 1.
    • Append either the first non-repeating character or # to the result.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

Initialize queue Q
Initialize frequency map freq\[26] = {0}
Initialize result string ans = ""

For each char c in stream:
freq\[c - 'a'] += 1
if freq\[c - 'a'] == 1:
Q.enqueue(c)

while Q is not empty and freq[Q.front - 'a'] > 1:
    Q.dequeue()

if Q is empty:
    ans += '#'
else:
    ans += Q.front

Return ans

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:


\[Start]
↓
For each character in stream:

* Increment frequency
* Add to queue if first occurrence
* While queue front is repeated → remove
* Append front of queue or '#'
  ↓
  \[End]

Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    public String FirstNonRepeating(String s) {
        int[] count = new int[26];  // To track character frequencies
        Queue<Character> q = new LinkedList<>();  // Queue for processing
        StringBuilder ans = new StringBuilder();

        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            count[ch - 'a']++;  // Update frequency

            // If this is the first occurrence, add to queue
            if (count[ch - 'a'] == 1) {
                q.add(ch);
            }

            // Remove characters from queue if they are no longer unique
            while (!q.isEmpty() && count[q.peek() - 'a'] > 1) {
                q.poll();
            }

            // Append first non-repeating character or #
            ans.append(q.isEmpty() ? '#' : q.peek());
        }
        return ans.toString();
    }
}

Time Complexity

  • O(N) (Each character is added and removed from the queue at most once)

Space Complexity

  • O(N) (Queue stores unique characters, worst case all distinct)

Notes:

  • The queue only ever contains unique candidates for the first non-repeating character.
  • Efficient for real-time stream processing.

Problem Statement: 166¶

Reverse First K Elements of Queue

Given an integer K and a queue of integers, reverse the order of the first K elements while keeping the rest in the same relative order.

  • Only the following operations are allowed:
    • enqueue(x): Add an item x to the rear of the queue.
    • dequeue(): Remove an item from the front of the queue.
    • size(): Returns the number of elements in the queue.
    • front(): Finds the front item.

Explanation

  • The first 3 elements [1, 2, 3] are reversed to [3, 2, 1].
  • The remaining [4, 5] stay the same.

Example
Input:


Queue: 1 2 3 4 5
K = 3

Output:


3 2 1 4 5

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ K ≤ N
  • 1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
  • Elements of the queue are integers in range [1, 10^6]

Goal:
Reverse only the first K elements of the queue without disturbing the order of the remaining elements.

Approach 1. Using a Stack and Queue (O(N))

  1. Extract the first K elements from the queue and push them into a stack.
  2. Pop elements from the stack and enqueue them back to the queue (this reverses the order).
  3. Move the remaining elements (n-k) to the back of the queue to maintain the original relative order.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:


\[Start]
↓
Push first K elements into stack
↓
Pop all from stack and enqueue (reversed)
↓
Move (N-K) elements from front to back
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function reverseFirstK(queue, K):
stack = new Stack()

for i from 0 to K-1:
    stack.push(queue.dequeue())

while stack is not empty:
    queue.enqueue(stack.pop())

for i from 0 to size(queue) - K:
    queue.enqueue(queue.dequeue())

return queue

Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class GfG {
    // Function to reverse first k elements of a queue.
    public Queue<Integer> modifyQueue(Queue<Integer> q, int k) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        
        // Step 1: Push first K elements into a stack
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            stack.push(q.poll());
        }
        
        // Step 2: Pop elements from stack and enqueue back (Reversed order)
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            q.add(stack.pop());
        }
        
        // Step 3: Move the remaining (n-k) elements to maintain relative order
        int size = q.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < size - k; i++) {
            q.add(q.poll());
        }
        
        return q;
    }
}

Time Complexity

  • O(K) + O(K) + O(N-K) = O(N)

Space Complexity

  • O(K) (Stack stores first K elements)

Notes:

  • Efficiently maintains queue order beyond the first K elements.
  • Uses standard queue operations; fits well with abstract data type constraints.

Problem Statement: 167¶

Minimum Cost of Ropes

Given an array arr[] representing the lengths of ropes, the goal is to connect all ropes into a single rope with the minimum total cost. The cost of connecting two ropes is the sum of their lengths. The process continues until one single rope is formed.

Explanation

  1. Pick 2 and 3, cost = 2+3=5, new array: [4, 5, 6]
  2. Pick 4 and 5, cost = 4+5=9, new array: [6, 9]
  3. Pick 6 and 9, cost = 6+9=15, new array: [15]
  4. Total cost = 5+9+15 = 29

Example
Input:

arr\[] = {4, 3, 2, 6}

Output:

29

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
  • 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10^6

Goal:
Minimize the total cost required to connect all the ropes into one.

Approach 1. Using Min-Heap (O(N log N))

  1. Push all elements into a Min-Heap (Priority Queue).
  2. Extract the two smallest elements, compute the cost, and insert the new rope back.
  3. Repeat until one rope remains.
  4. Sum all costs to get the minimum.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Build Min-Heap from input array
↓
while heap size > 1:
extract two smallest
calculate sum
add cost to total
insert sum back to heap
↓
return totalCost

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function minCost(arr):
create minHeap and insert all elements
totalCost = 0

while size of minHeap > 1:
    first = extractMin(minHeap)
    second = extractMin(minHeap)
    cost = first + second
    totalCost += cost
    insert(minHeap, cost)

return totalCost

Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    // Function to return the minimum cost of connecting the ropes.
    public int minCost(int[] arr) {
        // Min-Heap to get smallest elements first
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
        for (int num : arr) {
            pq.add(num);
        }
        
        int totalCost = 0;
        
        while (pq.size() > 1) {
            int first = pq.poll();
            int second = pq.poll();
            
            int sum = first + second;
            totalCost += sum;
            
            pq.add(sum);
        }
        
        return totalCost;
    }
}

Time Complexity

  • O(N log N)
    • Heap operations (O(log N)) happen N-1 times.
  • Efficient for large inputs!

Space Complexity

  • O(N) (For heap storage)

Notes:

  • Min-Heap ensures optimal greedy selection of the smallest ropes first.
  • Frequently used in file merging and network design problems.

Problem Statement: 168¶

Nearly Sorted Array Given an array arr[], where each element is at most k positions away from its target position in a sorted order, sort the array optimally.

Constraints

  • The array is not completely unsorted but has elements displaced by at most k positions.
  • Sorting should be in-place.

Explanation Each element is misplaced by at most 3 positions. We use a Min-Heap to efficiently sort.

Example
Input:

arr\[] = {6, 5, 3, 2, 8, 10, 9}, k = 3

Output:

{2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10}

Goal:
Efficiently sort the array using the information that elements are displaced by at most k positions.

Approach 1. Min-Heap (O(N log K))

  1. Use a Min-Heap (Priority Queue) to store at most k+1 elements.
  2. Insert the first k+1 elements into the heap.
  3. Iterate over the rest of the array:
    • Extract the smallest element and place it in the sorted order.
    • Insert the next element from the array into the heap.
  4. Empty the heap for remaining elements.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Insert first k+1 elements into Min-Heap
↓
For each remaining element:
→ Remove min from heap and place in array
→ Add current element to heap
↓
After array traversal:
→ Remove remaining elements from heap and place in array
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function nearlySorted(arr, k):
create a Min-Heap
for i = 0 to k:
heap.insert(arr\[i])
index = 0
for i = k+1 to end of arr:
arr\[index++] = heap.removeMin()
heap.insert(arr\[i])
while heap is not empty:
arr\[index++] = heap.removeMin()

Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    public void nearlySorted(int[] arr, int k) {
        int n = arr.length;
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();

        // Add first k+1 elements into the min-heap
        for (int i = 0; i <= k && i < n; i++) {
            pq.add(arr[i]);
        }

        int index = 0;

        // Process remaining elements
        for (int i = k + 1; i < n; i++) {
            arr[index++] = pq.poll();
            pq.add(arr[i]);
        }

        // Empty the remaining elements from the heap
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            arr[index++] = pq.poll();
        }
    }
}

Time Complexity

  • Insertion & Deletion in Min-Heap → O(log k)
  • Processing N elements → O(N log k)
  • Overall Complexity → O(N log k) (much better than O(N log N) sorting)

Space Complexity

  • O(k) (Heap stores at most k+1 elements)

Notes:

  • Optimized for partially sorted data.
  • Frequently used in streaming and real-time processing scenarios where sorting windows of data efficiently is needed.

Problem Statement: 170¶

Max Sum Subarray of Size K Given an array of integers arr[] and a number k, return the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray of size k.

Input:

  • An integer array arr[] (positive/negative integers).
  • An integer k (size of the subarray).

Output:

  • The maximum sum of a contiguous subarray of size k.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= k <= arr.length <= 10^5
  • -10^4 <= arr[i] <= 10^4

Example
Input:

arr\[] = {100, 200, 300, 400}, k = 2

Output:

700

Goal of the Code: To efficiently find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size k using an optimized approach.

Approach:

  1. Use Sliding Window Technique.
  2. Calculate the sum of the first window of size k.
  3. For each subsequent element, slide the window by:
    • Removing the element that is moving out of the window.
    • Adding the new element coming into the window.
  4. Track the maximum sum encountered.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Calculate sum of first k elements → current\_sum
↓
Initialize result = current\_sum
↓
For each i = k to n-1:
current\_sum = current\_sum + arr\[i] - arr\[i-k]
result = max(result, current\_sum)
↓
Return result
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize result and current_sum as the sum of the first window of size k.
  2. Traverse the array from index k to n:
    • Update current_sum by adding arr[i] and removing arr[i - k].
    • Update result if current_sum is greater.
  3. Return result.

Code:

// User function Template for Java

class Solution {
    public int maximumSumSubarray(int[] arr, int k) {
        // Code here
        if(arr.length<k){
            return -1;
        }
        
        int res=0;
        for(int i=0; i<k; i++){
            res+=arr[i];
        }
        
        int curr_sum=res;
        for(int i=k; i<arr.length; i++){
            curr_sum+=arr[i]-arr[i-k];
            res=Math.max(res,curr_sum);
        }
        
        return res;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity:

  • Time Complexity: O(N) (Single traversal of the array).
  • Space Complexity: O(1) (Constant space for variables).

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • This approach ensures an optimal solution using sliding window technique rather than brute force.

Notes:

  • This method avoids recomputation of overlapping elements in the subarray.
  • Efficient for large arrays where k << N.

Problem Statement: 169¶

Count Distinct Elements in Every Window

Given an integer array arr[] and a number k, find the count of distinct elements in every window of size k in the array.

Input:

  • An integer array arr[] of size n
  • An integer k representing the size of the window

Output:

  • A list of integers representing the count of distinct elements in each window of size k.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= n <= 10^5
  • 1 <= k <= n
  • 0 <= arr[i] <= 10^5

Example
Input:

arr\[] = {1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 3}, k = 4

Output:

3 4 4 3

Goal of the Code: To efficiently find and count the number of distinct elements within every window of size k using an optimized approach.

Approach:

  1. Use a Hash Map to keep track of element frequencies within the current window.
  2. Slide the window by one element at a time:
    • Add the next element to the map.
    • Remove the frequency of the element that is sliding out of the window.
    • Track the count of distinct elements by checking the size of the map.
  3. Continue until the end of the array.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Initialize freq map and result list
↓
Add first k elements to map
↓
Add map size to result
↓
For i = k to n-1:

* Increment freq of arr\[i]
* Decrement freq of arr\[i - k]
* Remove if freq becomes 0
* Add map size to result
  ↓
  Return result
  ↓
  \[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize a Hash Map to keep track of element frequencies.
  2. Traverse the first k elements and update the map.
  3. For each subsequent element:
    • Add the new element to the map.
    • Reduce the count of the outgoing element in the map.
    • If the count of the outgoing element becomes zero, remove it from the map.
    • Store the size of the map as the result for the current window.
  4. Return the results.

Code:

class Solution {
    ArrayList<Integer> countDistinct(int arr[], int k) {
        // code here
        int n=arr.length;
        ArrayList<Integer> res=new ArrayList<>();
        Map<Integer, Integer> freq=new HashMap<>();
        
        for(int i=0; i<k; i++){
            freq.put(arr[i],freq.getOrDefault(arr[i],0)+1);
        }
        
        res.add(freq.size());
        
        for(int i=k; i<n; i++){
            freq.put(arr[i],freq.getOrDefault(arr[i],0)+1);
            freq.put(arr[i-k], freq.get(arr[i-k])-1);
            
            if(freq.get(arr[i-k])==0){
                freq.remove(arr[i-k]);
            }
            res.add(freq.size());
        }
        
        return res;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity:

  • Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the size of the array. Each insertion and deletion operation in the map takes O(1) on average.
  • Space Complexity: O(K) where K is the size of the window (size of the hash map).

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • Use a sliding window technique to ensure we only make changes for elements entering or leaving the window.

Notes:

  • HashMap ensures constant-time updates.
  • Efficient for large arrays compared to nested loops.

Problem Statement: 171¶

First Negative Integer in Every Window of Size K

Given an array arr[] and a positive integer k, find the first negative integer in each and every contiguous subarray (window) of size k.

If a window does not contain a negative integer, return 0 for that window.

Input:

  • An integer array arr[] (contains positive/negative integers).
  • An integer k (size of the subarray/window).

Output:

  • A list of integers representing the first negative number in every window of size k. If no negative number exists, return 0.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= k <= arr.length <= 10^5
  • -10^4 <= arr[i] <= 10^4

Example

Input:

arr\[] = {12, -1, -7, 8, 15, 30, 16, 28}, k = 3

Output:

-1 -1 -7 -1 0 0

Explanation:

  • Window 1: {12, -1, -7} → First negative = -1
  • Window 2: {-1, -7, 8} → First negative = -1
  • Window 3: {-7, 8, 15} → First negative = -7
  • Window 4: {8, 15, 30} → First negative = 0
  • Window 5: {15, 30, 16} → First negative = 0
  • Window 6: {30, 16, 28} → First negative = 0

Diagram:


| Window        | First Negative |
| ------------- | -------------- |
| \[12, -1, -7] | -1             |
| \[-1, -7, 8]  | -1             |
| \[-7, 8, 15]  | -7             |
| \[8, 15, 30]  | 0              |
| \[15, 30, 16] | 0              |
| \[30, 16, 28] | 0              |

Goal of the Code: To efficiently find the first negative integer in each window using an optimized approach.

Approach:

  1. Use Sliding Window Technique with a Deque (Double-Ended Queue).
  2. Traverse the array while maintaining a deque to store indices of negative numbers.
  3. For each window of size k:
    • If the front of the deque is out of the current window, remove it.
    • Add the current index if the element is negative.
    • Store the first negative integer (if present) or 0 if no negative integer exists.
  4. Continue until all windows are processed.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Initialize deque to store indices of negative numbers.
  • Traverse first k elements, enqueue indices of negative numbers.
  • Slide window from k to end:
    • Record front of deque (first negative in window) or 0 if empty.
    • Remove indices out of current window from deque front.
    • Add current element index if negative.
  • Record result for last window.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Create empty deque dq.
  2. For i in 0 to k-1:
    • If arr[i] is negative, add i to dq.
  3. For i in k to n-1:
    • If dq not empty, add arr[dq.front()] to result else add 0.
    • Remove indices from dq front if they are out of current window (i-k).
    • If arr[i] is negative, add i to dq.
  4. After loop, add first negative integer or 0 for last window.
  5. Return result list.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize a Deque<Integer> to store indices of negative numbers.
  2. Traverse the first k elements:
    • If the element is negative, store its index in the deque.
  3. Process the remaining elements:
    • Remove indices that are out of the current window.
    • Add the new element’s index if it is negative.
    • Store arr[deque.peek()] if deque is not empty, else store 0.
  4. Return the result list.

Code:

class Solution {
    static List<Integer> firstNegInt(int arr[], int k) {
        // write code here
        Deque<Integer> dq=new LinkedList<>();
        List<Integer> res=new ArrayList<>();
        int n=arr.length;
        
        for(int i=0; i<k; i++){
            if(arr[i]<0) dq.addLast(i);
        }
        
        for(int i=k; i<n; i++ ){
            
            if(!dq.isEmpty()) res.add(arr[dq.peekFirst()]);
            else res.add(0);
            
            while(!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <=i-k){
                dq.pollFirst();
            }
            
               // Add the new element (if within bounds)
            if (i < n && arr[i] < 0) dq.addLast(i);
            }
            
             if(!dq.isEmpty()) res.add(arr[dq.peekFirst()]);
            else res.add(0);
 
 return res;           
}
}

Time Complexity:
O(N) - each element is processed once when added or removed from the deque.

Space Complexity:
O(K) - deque stores indices of negative elements in current window, at most k elements.

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • This approach ensures an optimal solution using sliding window technique rather than brute force.
  • Deque operations (insertion/removal from both ends) are O(1), making the approach highly efficient.
  • Works well even with large arrays due to linear complexity.

Problem Statement: 172¶

K Sized Subarray Maximum

Given an array arr[] of integers and an integer k, find the maximum value for each contiguous subarray of size k. The output should be an array of maximum values corresponding to each contiguous subarray.

Input:

  • An integer array arr[].
  • An integer k (size of the subarray).

Output:

  • An array containing the maximum values of all contiguous subarrays of size k.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= k <= arr.length <= 10^5
  • -10^4 <= arr[i] <= 10^4

Example Input: arr = [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7] k = 3

Output: [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]

Explanation: Subarrays of size 3: [1,3,-1] -> max = 3 [3,-1,-3] -> max = 3 [-1,-3,5] -> max = 5 [-3,5,3] -> max = 5 [5,3,6] -> max = 6 [3,6,7] -> max = 7

Goal of the Code: To efficiently find the maximum element in each contiguous subarray of size k using an optimized approach.

Approach:

  1. Use a Deque (Double-Ended Queue) to efficiently track the maximum value in each window.
  2. Process the first k elements:
    • Remove elements from the back of the deque that are smaller than the current element.
    • Add the current index to the deque.
  3. For each subsequent element:
    • Store the front element of the deque as the maximum for the previous window.
    • Remove indices that are out of the current window.
    • Remove elements from the back that are smaller than the current element.
    • Add the current index to the deque.
  4. Store the maximum of the last window.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Initialize deque to store indices in decreasing order of values.
  • Process first k elements:
    • Remove smaller elements from back of deque.
    • Add current index.
  • Slide window from k to end:
    • Add front of deque to results (maximum for previous window).
    • Remove indices out of current window from front.
    • Remove smaller elements from back.
    • Add current index.
  • Add maximum for last window.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize empty deque dq.
  2. For i in 0 to k-1:
    • While dq not empty and arr[i] >= arr[dq.last()], remove last from dq.
    • Add i to dq.
  3. For i in k to n-1:
    • Append arr[dq.first()] to result.
    • Remove indices from front if out of window (i-k).
    • While dq not empty and arr[i] >= arr[dq.last()], remove last from dq.
    • Add i to dq.
  4. Append arr[dq.first()] to result for last window.
  5. Return result.

Code:

class Solution {
    static ArrayList<Integer> maxOfSubarrays(int[] arr, int k) {
        // code here
        int n=arr.length;
        ArrayList<Integer> res=new ArrayList<>();
        Deque<Integer> dq=new ArrayDeque<>();
        
        for(int i=0; i<k; i++){
            while(!dq.isEmpty() && arr[i]>=arr[dq.peekLast()]){
                dq.pollLast();
            }
            dq.addLast(i);
        }
        
        for(int i=k; i<n; i++){
            res.add(arr[dq.peekFirst()]);
            
            while(!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i-k){
                dq.pollFirst();
            }
            
             while(!dq.isEmpty() && arr[i]>=arr[dq.peekLast()]){
                dq.pollLast();
            }
            dq.addLast(i);
            
        }
        
        res.add(arr[dq.peekFirst()]);
        
        return res;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity:

  • Time Complexity: O(N) (Each element is processed once).
  • Space Complexity: O(K) (For the deque storing indices).

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • The use of a deque ensures that each element is processed in constant time.
  • This approach is much more efficient than brute force O(N*K) solutions.

Notes:

  • Deque stores indices of elements in decreasing order of their values.
  • Ensures O(N) time by processing each element once.

Problem Statement: 173¶

Substrings of Length K with K-1 Distinct Elements

Given a string S consisting of only lowercase alphabets and an integer K, find the count of all substrings of length K which have exactly K-1 distinct characters.

Input:

  • A string S of lowercase alphabets.
  • An integer K (length of the substring).

Output:

  • An integer representing the count of substrings of length K with exactly K-1 distinct characters.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= K <= S.length <= 10^5
  • S consists of only lowercase English letters.

Example Input: S = "aabab" K = 3

Output: 3

Explanation: Substrings of length 3 are:

  • "aab" -> distinct chars = 2 (a,b) -> 3-1=2 ✓
  • "aba" -> distinct chars = 2 (a,b) -> 3-1=2 ✓
  • "bab" -> distinct chars = 2 (a,b) -> 3-1=2 ✓

Count = 3

Goal of the Code: To efficiently count the number of substrings of length K that contain exactly K-1 distinct characters using an optimized approach.

Approach:

  1. Use a sliding window technique along with a frequency array to track character occurrences.
  2. Process the first K-1 characters and store their frequencies.
  3. For each subsequent character:
    • Add the current character to the frequency map.
    • Count distinct characters.
    • If the distinct count is exactly K-1, increment the result.
    • Remove the first character of the previous window from the frequency map.
  4. Return the final count of valid substrings.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Initialize frequency array of size 26.
  • Process first K-1 characters to populate frequency.
  • Slide window from K-1 to end:
    • Add current character frequency.
    • Count distinct characters in frequency array.
    • If distinct count equals K-1, increment result.
    • Remove frequency of character leaving the window.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize frequency array count[26] = 0.
  2. For i in 0 to K-2: increment frequency of S[i].
  3. For i in K-1 to n-1:
    • Increment frequency of S[i].
    • Count distinct characters in count.
    • If distinct == K-1, increment answer.
    • Decrement frequency of S[i-K+1].
  4. Return answer.

Code:

//User function Template for Java

class Solution {
    static int countOfSubstrings(String S, int K) {
        // code here
        
        int n=S.length();
        int[] count=new int[26];
        int ans=0;
        
        if(K>n) return 0;
        
        for(int i=0; i<K-1; i++){
            count[S.charAt(i)-'a']++;
        }
        
        for(int i=K-1; i<n; i++){
            count[S.charAt(i)-'a']++;
            
            int distinctCnt=0;
            for(int j1=0; j1<26; j1++){
                if(count[j1]>0) distinctCnt++;
            }
            
            if(distinctCnt==K-1) ans++;
            
            count[S.charAt(i-K+1)-'a']--;
        }
        
        return ans;
        
    }
};

Time and Space Complexity:

  • Time Complexity: O(N), as we iterate through the string once.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), since we use a fixed-size frequency array (26 letters).

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • The sliding window technique ensures efficient traversal of the string without redundant calculations.
  • Using an array for character frequencies is more efficient than using a HashMap.

Notes:

  • Counting distinct characters inside the loop can be optimized using a variable to track distinct count dynamically instead of scanning all 26 characters each time, improving efficiency.

Problem Statement: 185¶

Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size

Given an array of integers arr[], find the maximum of the minimum values for every possible window size in the array.

More formally, for each window size k, determine the smallest element in all windows of size k, and then find the largest value among these minimums, where 1 ≤ k ≤ arr.length.

Input:

  • An array arr[] of integers.

Output:

  • A list of integers where the i-th element represents the maximum of the minimum values for all windows of size i+1.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 10^5
  • -10^6 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10^6

Example:

Input:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 50, 10, 70, 30]

Output:
[70, 30, 20, 10, 10, 10, 10]

Explanation:
For window size 1: max of [10,20,30,50,10,70,30] = 70  
For window size 2: min of each pair = [10,20,30,10,10,30] → max = 30  
For window size 3: min of windows = [10,20,10,10,10] → max = 20  
... and so on.

Goal of the Code:
To efficiently determine the maximum of minimum values for every possible window size using the Monotonic Stack + Dynamic Programming technique.

Approach
The problem can be efficiently solved using monotonic stacks and window size mapping:

  1. Key Idea:

    • Compute the next smaller element (NSE) and previous smaller element (PSE) for each index.
    • Use this to determine the window size where an element is the minimum.
    • Fill a result array where res[k] stores the maximum of minimums for window size k+1.

  2. Steps to Solve:

    • Use a monotonic stack to find next smaller element (NSE) and previous smaller element (PSE).
    • Compute the window size where each element is the minimum.
    • Use a result array res[] to track the maximum of minimums.
    • Process res[] from right to left to ensure the correct values are filled.

flowchart TD

A[Start with arr[] of size N] --> B[Initialize arrays: left[], right[], res[]]
    B --> C[Use Monotonic Stack to compute Previous Smaller Element (PSE)]
    C --> D[Use Monotonic Stack to compute Next Smaller Element (NSE)]
    D --> E[Calculate window size for each element: len = right[i] - left[i] - 1]
    E --> F[Update res[len - 1] = max(res[len - 1], arr[i])]
    F --> G[Fill remaining res[] from right to left to maintain max values]
    G --> H[Return res[]]

Pseudocode/Algorithm

  1. Initialize stacks and arrays for next smaller and previous smaller elements.
  2. Use monotonic stack to compute NSE and PSE.
  3. Compute the window size for each element and store its minimum value.
  4. Process res[] to ensure correct values for all window sizes.
  5. Return the result array.

Java Solution

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    public ArrayList<Integer> maxOfMins(int[] arr) {
        int n = arr.length;
        
        ArrayList<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(n, 0));
        Stack<Integer> s = new Stack<>();
        ArrayList<Integer> lenArr = new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(n, 0));
        
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            while (!s.isEmpty() && arr[s.peek()] >= arr[i]) {
                int top = s.pop();
                int windowSize = s.isEmpty() ? i : i - s.peek() - 1;
                lenArr.set(top, windowSize);
            }
            s.push(i);
        }
        
        while (!s.isEmpty()) {
            int top = s.pop();
            int windowSize = s.isEmpty() ? n : n - s.peek() - 1;
            lenArr.set(top, windowSize);
        }
        
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int windowSize = lenArr.get(i) - 1;
            res.set(windowSize, Math.max(res.get(windowSize), arr[i]));
        }
        
        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
            res.set(i, Math.max(res.get(i), res.get(i + 1)));
        }
        
        return res;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(N), since each element is pushed and popped from the stack at most once.
  • Space Complexity: O(N), for storing window sizes and results.

Notes:

  • This problem is best solved using the concept of Next Smaller Element (NSE) and Previous Smaller Element (PSE).
  • For each element, we find the largest window in which it is the minimum, and map it accordingly.
  • Post-processing ensures that if a window of size k has no entry, it inherits from larger windows (since max of min is non-increasing).

Problem Statement: 174¶

Indexes of Subarray Sum

Given an array arr[] containing only non-negative integers, your task is to find a continuous subarray (a contiguous sequence of elements) whose sum equals a specified value target. You need to return the 1-based indices of the leftmost and rightmost elements of this subarray. If no such subarray is found, return [-1].

Input:

  • An integer array arr[] containing non-negative integers.
  • An integer target representing the desired sum.

Output:

  • A list containing the 1-based indices [left, right] of the first subarray whose sum equals target.
  • If no subarray is found, return [-1].

Constraints:

  • 1 <= arr.length <= 10^5
  • 0 <= arr[i] <= 10^5
  • 1 <= target <= 10^9

Example

Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 7, 5], target = 12

Output: [2, 4]

Explanation: The subarray [2, 3, 7] has a sum of 12. The 1-based indices are 2 to 4.

Goal of the Code: To efficiently find the first contiguous subarray whose sum equals target using an optimized approach.

Approach:

  1. Use the Sliding Window (Two-Pointer) Technique to maintain a running sum of the subarray.
  2. Start with two pointers (start and end) and a variable curr_sum initialized to 0.
  3. Iterate through the array:
    • Expand the window by adding the current element to curr_sum.
    • If curr_sum exceeds target, shrink the window from the left by removing elements until curr_sum <= target.
    • If curr_sum == target, return the 1-based indices [start+1, end+1].
  4. If no subarray is found, return [-1].

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

flowchart TD
    A[Start] --> B[Initialize start=0, curr_sum=0]
    B --> C[Loop through array with end pointer]
    C --> D[Add arr[end] to curr_sum]
    D --> E{curr_sum > target?}
    E -- Yes --> F[Subtract arr[start] from curr_sum, increment start]
    F --> E
    E -- No --> G{curr_sum == target?}
    G -- Yes --> H[Return [start+1, end+1]]
    G -- No --> I[Continue loop]
    I --> C
    C --> J[If no subarray found, return [-1]]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize start = 0, curr_sum = 0.
  2. Traverse the array using end pointer:
    • Add arr[end] to curr_sum.
    • While curr_sum > target, subtract arr[start] and increment start.
    • If curr_sum == target, return [start+1, end+1].
  3. If no subarray is found, return [-1].

Code:

class Solution {
    static ArrayList<Integer> subarraySum(int[] arr, int target) {
        // code here
        int s=0, e=0;
        ArrayList<Integer> res=new ArrayList<>();
        int cur=0;
        for(int i=0; i<arr.length; i++){
            cur+=arr[i];
            if(cur>=target){
                e=i;
                while(cur > target && s < e){
                    cur-=arr[s];
                    s++;
                }
                
                if(cur==target){
                    res.add(s+1);
                    res.add(e+1);
                    return res;
                }
            }
        }
        res.add(-1);
        return res;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity:

  • Time Complexity: O(N), as each element is processed at most twice (once added, once removed).
  • Space Complexity: O(1), as only a few extra variables are used.

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • The sliding window approach ensures an efficient solution compared to brute force methods (O(N^2)).
  • The algorithm works optimally for both small and large target values.

Problem Statement: 175¶

Subarray with 0 Sum

Given an array of integers arr[], determine if there is a subarray (of size at least one) with a sum equal to 0. Return true if such a subarray exists, otherwise return false.

Input:

  • An integer array arr[] of size n.

Output:

  • A boolean value (true or false) indicating whether a subarray with sum 0 exists.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= n <= 10^5
  • -10^5 <= arr[i] <= 10^5

Example

Input: arr = [4, 2, -3, 1, 6]

Output: true

Explanation: The subarray [2, -3, 1] sums to 0, so a subarray with 0 sum exists.

Goal of the Code: To efficiently check if any subarray within the given array has a sum of 0 using an optimized approach.

Approach:

  1. Use a Hash Set to store the cumulative sum encountered so far.
  2. Iterate through the array while maintaining a running sum.
  3. If at any point: then a subarray with sum 0 exists.
    • The current element is 0, or
    • The cumulative sum becomes 0, or
    • The cumulative sum has been seen before in the set,
  4. If no such subarray is found, return false.

🧮Flowchart/ Diagram:

flowchart TD
    A[Start] --> B[Initialize sum = 0, empty hash set]
    B --> C[Traverse the array]
    C --> D[Add current element to sum]
    D --> E{sum == 0 or arr[i] == 0 or sum in set?}
    E -- Yes --> F[Return true]
    E -- No --> G[Add sum to hash set]
    G --> C
    C --> H[If loop ends, return false]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize an empty Hash Set and a variable sum = 0.
  2. Traverse through the array:
    • Add arr[i] to sum.
    • If sum == 0 or arr[i] == 0 or sum is already in the set, return true.
    • Otherwise, add sum to the set.
  3. If loop completes without finding a zero-sum subarray, return false.

Code:

class Solution {
    // Function to check whether there is a subarray present with 0-sum or not.
    static boolean findsum(int arr[]) {
        // Your code here
        Set<Integer> hs=new HashSet<Integer>();
        int sum=0;
        for(int i=0; i<arr.length; i++){
            sum+=arr[i];
            
            if(arr[i]==0 || sum==0 || hs.contains(sum)){
                return true;
            }
        
        hs.add(sum);
        
        }
        
        return false;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity:

  • Time Complexity: O(N), as we traverse the array once.
  • Space Complexity: O(N), due to the usage of a Hash Set.

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • The Hash Set is used to track previous cumulative sums efficiently.
  • If the same cumulative sum appears again, it means the intermediate sum between two indices is 0, confirming a zero-sum subarray.

Problem Statement: 189¶

Smallest Distinct Window

Given a string s, find the length of the smallest window that contains all the characters of the given string at least once.

Input:

  • A string s consisting of lowercase and uppercase English letters.

Output:

  • An integer representing the length of the smallest substring that contains all distinct characters in s.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10^5

Example

Input: s = "AABBC"

Output: 3

Explanation: The distinct characters in "AABBC" are 'A', 'B', and 'C'. The substring "ABC" is the smallest window containing all these distinct characters.

Goal of the Code:
To efficiently determine the smallest substring length that contains all unique characters of s at least once, using the Sliding Window (Two Pointers) Technique.

Approach
The problem can be efficiently solved using a sliding window approach with two pointers:

  1. Key Idea:

    • The number of distinct characters in s is fixed (distinct).
    • Use a frequency map (count[]) to track occurrences of characters in the current window.
    • Expand the window (end++) to include all distinct characters.
    • Once all distinct characters are in the window (matched == distinct), try to shrink it (start++) while maintaining all distinct characters.
    • Update the minimum window length found.

  2. Steps to Solve:

    • Compute distinct, the number of unique characters in s.
    • Use a frequency array count[256] to track character counts.
    • Expand the window (end++) while maintaining a count of matched distinct characters.
    • Once all distinct characters are in the window, try shrinking it from the left (start++).
    • Keep track of the smallest window size found.

Flowchart

flowchart TD
    A[Start] --> B[Count total distinct characters in the string]
    B --> C[Initialize count array, start, end, matched, minLen]
    C --> D[Increment count of s[end] and move end forward]
    D --> E{Have all distinct chars been matched?}
    E -- No --> D
    E -- Yes --> F[Update minLen if current window is smaller]
    F --> G[Decrease count of s[start] and move start forward]
    G --> H{Still all matched?}
    H -- Yes --> F
    H -- No --> D
    D --> I[Repeat until end of string]
    I --> J[Return minLen]

Pseudocode/Algorithm

  1. Compute distinct = count of unique characters in s.
  2. Initialize start = 0, minLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE, and matched = 0.
  3. Use count[256] to track occurrences of characters in the current window.
  4. Expand the window (end++) until all distinct characters are included.
  5. Once matched == distinct:
    • Try shrinking the window from start++.
    • Update minLen if the current window is smaller.
    • If removing s[start] reduces matched, stop shrinking.
  6. Return minLen as the smallest distinct window length.

Java Solution

import java.io.*;

class Solution {
    public int findSubString(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        if (n <= 1) return n;

        int[] count = new int[256];
        int distinct = (int) s.chars().distinct().count();
        int start = 0, startIdx = -1, matched = 0, minLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

        for (int end = 0; end < n; end++) {
            if (++count[s.charAt(end)] == 1) matched++;

            while (matched == distinct) {
                if (end - start + 1 < minLen) {
                    minLen = end - start + 1;
                    startIdx = start;
                }
                if (--count[s.charAt(start++)] == 0) matched--;
            }
        }
        return startIdx == -1 ? -1 : minLen;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(N), since each character is processed at most twice (once for expansion, once for contraction).
  • Space Complexity: O(1), since we use a fixed frequency array of size 256 (constant space).

Additional Notes/Hints:

  • This problem is a classic variant of the minimum window substring type problem, with a simplified condition: we just need to include all unique characters, not match a target pattern.
  • Using an array of size 256 (ASCII range) ensures constant space for character frequency tracking.
  • Carefully maintaining the matched count avoids repeatedly checking the whole count array, which helps keep the time complexity linear.
  • The shrinking phase of the sliding window is crucial to minimizing the window size efficiently.
  • If all characters in the string are already unique, the result is the length of the string itself.

Problem Statement: 186¶

Smallest Window Containing 0, 1, and 2

Given a string S consisting of the characters '0', '1', and '2', find the length of the smallest substring that contains all three characters.

If no such substring exists, return -1.

Input:

  • A string S containing only the characters '0', '1', and '2'.

Output:

  • An integer representing the length of the smallest substring containing 0, 1, and 2.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ S.length ≤ 10^5
  • S[i] ∈ {'0', '1', '2'}

Example: Input:
S = "121203"

Output:
3

Explanation:
The smallest substring containing '0', '1', and '2' is "120" (indices 2 to 4, 1-based), length 3.

Goal of the Code:
To efficiently determine the minimum-length substring that contains 0, 1, and 2 using the Sliding Window (Two Pointers) Technique.

Approach
The problem can be efficiently solved using a sliding window approach:

  1. Key Idea:

    • Use a frequency array to track the count of '0', '1', and '2' in the current window.
    • Expand the right pointer (k) until all three characters are present.
    • Once found, try shrinking the window from the left (i) while maintaining all three characters.
    • Keep track of the smallest window length found.

  2. Steps to Solve:

    • Use two pointers i (left) and k (right) to form a dynamic sliding window.
    • Use a frequency array of size 3 to count occurrences of '0', '1', and '2'.
    • Expand the right pointer k until the window contains all three characters.
    • Shrink the left pointer i to find the smallest valid window.
    • Return the minimum window size, or -1 if no such window exists.

Flowchart:

Start
  |
  v
Initialize i=0, k=0, cnt=0, freq[3]={0,0,0}, minLen=∞
  |
  v
While k < length of S:
  |
  v
  Increment freq[S[k]-'0']
  |
  v
  If freq[S[k]-'0'] == 1:
     Increment cnt
  |
  v
  If cnt == 3 (all characters present):
    |
    v
    While freq[S[i]-'0'] > 1:
      Decrement freq[S[i]-'0']
      Increment i
    |
    Update minLen = min(minLen, k - i + 1)
    Decrement freq[S[i]-'0']
    Increment i
    Decrement cnt
  |
  v
  Increment k
    |
    v
    End While
    |
    v
    If minLen == ∞:
    Return -1
    Else:
    Return minLen
    |
    v
    End

Pseudocode/Algorithm

  1. Initialize i = 0, k = 0, and cnt = 0 (count of distinct numbers in the window).
  2. Use an array freq[] of size 3 to track counts of '0', '1', '2'.
  3. Expand k and update freq[S[k] - '0'].
  4. If all three numbers exist in the window (cnt == 3), try shrinking i.
  5. Keep track of the minimum window length.
  6. Return the minimum window length, or -1 if not found.

Java Solution

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    public int smallestSubstring(String S) {
        int n = S.length(), i = 0, k = 0, cnt = 0;
        int minLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int[] freq = new int[3];
        Arrays.fill(freq, 0);
        
        while (k < n) {
            freq[S.charAt(k) - '0']++;
            if (freq[S.charAt(k) - '0'] == 1) {
                cnt++;
            }
            
            if (cnt == 3) {
                while (freq[S.charAt(i) - '0'] > 1) {
                    freq[S.charAt(i) - '0']--;
                    i++;
                }
                minLen = Math.min(minLen, k - i + 1);
                freq[S.charAt(i) - '0']--;
                i++;
                cnt--;
            }
            
            k++;
        }
        
        return (minLen == Integer.MAX_VALUE) ? -1 : minLen;
    }
}

Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(N), since each character is processed at most twice (once when expanding, once when shrinking).
  • Space Complexity: O(1), since we use only a fixed-size freq[] array of length 3.

Additional Notes:

  • The window is dynamically expanded and shrunk while maintaining the condition that all three characters exist.
  • The algorithm terminates after scanning the string once, ensuring O(N) time complexity.
  • Since only three characters are involved, space complexity remains O(1).

Problem Statement: 184¶

Smallest Window Containing All Characters of Another String

Given two strings s1 and s2, find the smallest window in s1 that contains all characters (including duplicates) of s2. If no such window exists, return "". If multiple windows of the same length exist, return the one with the smallest starting index.

Input:

  • A string s1 of lowercase English letters.
  • A string s2 of lowercase English letters.

Output:

  • A smallest substring in s1 that contains all characters of s2.
  • If no such substring exists, return "".

Constraints:

  • 1 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 10^5

Example: Input:
s1 = "timetopractice"
s2 = "toc"

Output:
"toprac"

Explanation:
The smallest window in s1 containing all characters of s2 (including duplicates) is "toprac".

Goal of the Code:
To efficiently find the smallest window that contains all characters of s2 using the Sliding Window (Two Pointers) Technique.

Approach
The problem can be efficiently solved using the Sliding Window + HashMap approach:

  1. Key Idea:

    • Maintain a frequency count of characters in s2.
    • Use two pointers (left and right) to expand/shrink the window dynamically.
    • When a valid window is found (i.e., it contains all characters of s2), try shrinking it to find the smallest one.

  2. Sliding Window Approach:

    • Expand the right pointer (right) to include characters from s1 while maintaining a count of matched characters.
    • If all characters from s2 are matched, shrink the left pointer (left) to find the smallest possible window.
    • Track the minimum window length and update the start index accordingly.

Flowchart:

Start
  |
  v
Initialize frequency map for s2 (hashP)
Initialize empty frequency map for s1 (hashS)
Initialize start=0, count=0, minLen=∞, startIdx=-1
  |
  v
For end in [0..len(s1)-1]:
  |
  v
  Add s1[end] to hashS frequency
  If s1[end] in hashP and hashS[s1[end]] <= hashP[s1[end]]:
    Increment count
  |
  v
  While count == length(s2):
    If current window smaller than minLen:
      Update minLen and startIdx
    Remove s1[start] from hashS frequency
    If s1[start] in hashP and hashS[s1[start]] < hashP[s1[start]]:
      Decrement count
    Increment start
  |
  v
End For
  |
  v
If startIdx == -1:
  Return ""
Else:
  Return substring(s1, startIdx, startIdx + minLen)
  |
  v
End

Pseudocode/Algorithm

  1. Initialize frequency maps for s2 and s1.
  2. Expand the right pointer, updating the frequency map for s1.
  3. When all characters from s2 are matched, shrink the left pointer.
  4. Track the smallest window length and starting index.
  5. Return the substring of s1 corresponding to the smallest window found.

Java Solution

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    public static String smallestWindow(String s1, String s2) {
        int len1 = s1.length(), len2 = s2.length();
        if (len1 < len2) return "";

        HashMap<Character, Integer> hashP = new HashMap<>();
        HashMap<Character, Integer> hashS = new HashMap<>();

        for (char c : s2.toCharArray()) {
            hashP.put(c, hashP.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
        }

        int start = 0, startIdx = -1, count = 0, minLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

        for (int end = 0; end < len1; end++) {
            char currentChar = s1.charAt(end);
            hashS.put(currentChar, hashS.getOrDefault(currentChar, 0) + 1);

            if (hashP.containsKey(currentChar) && hashS.get(currentChar) <= hashP.get(currentChar)) {
                count++;
            }

            while (count == len2) {
                if (end - start + 1 < minLen) {
                    minLen = end - start + 1;
                    startIdx = start;
                }

                char startChar = s1.charAt(start);
                hashS.put(startChar, hashS.get(startChar) - 1);
                if (hashP.containsKey(startChar) && hashS.get(startChar) < hashP.get(startChar)) {
                    count--;
                }
                start++;
            }
        }
        return startIdx == -1 ? "" : s1.substring(startIdx, startIdx + minLen);
    }
}

Code:2

public class SmallestWindow {
    public static String smallestWindow(String s, String p) {
        int len1 = s.length();
        int len2 = p.length();

        if (len1 < len2)
            return "-1";

        int[] countP = new int[256];
        int[] countS = new int[256];

        // Store occurrence of characters of P
        for (int i = 0; i < len2; i++)
            countP[p.charAt(i)]++;

        int start = 0, start_idx = -1, min_len = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int count = 0;

        for (int j = 0; j < len1; j++) {
            char currChar = s.charAt(j);
            
            // Count occurrence of characters of string S
            countS[currChar]++;

            // If S's char matches with P's char, increment count
            if (countP[currChar] > 0 && countS[currChar] <= countP[currChar]) {
                count++;
            }

            // If all characters are matched
            if (count == len2) {
                
                // Try to minimize the window
                char startChar;
                while (countS[startChar = s.charAt(start)] > countP[startChar] || countP[startChar] == 0) {
                    if (countS[startChar] > countP[startChar]) {
                        countS[startChar]--;
                    }
                    start++;
                }

                // Update window size
                int len = j - start + 1;
